newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's Lebed faces Cold War foes on NATO trip.
newsitem.headline: Russia's Lebed faces Cold War foes on NATO trip.

text.p: Sabre-rattling security tsar Alexander Lebed comes face-to-face with his former Cold War foes next week when he visits NATO headquarters to explain Russia's opposition to the alliance's enlargement plans.

On his first trip to the West, Lebed will have potentially explosive meetings in Brussels with leaders of an organisation which he has threatened with rusty Russian rockets if it expands to include countries of eastern and central Europe.

"NATO's expansion eastwards will take us back to hostility and to the spirit of confrontation," Lebed, who is now President Boris Yeltsin's national security adviser, told reporters on Tuesday in comments that can hardly encourage alliance chiefs.
"We have missiles, which are rusty but still effective, as a deterrent argument."

Lebed flies to Brussels on Sunday at NATO's invitation. He is expected to have talks with NATO Secretary General Javier Solana on Monday and with General George Joulwan, Supreme Allied Commander of NATO Forces in Europe, on Tuesday.

The 46-year-old former paratroop general says he has only once before been out of the former Soviet Union -- when he fought in Afghanistan in the 1980s -- because he knew too many military secrets to be allowed to travel.
Russian opinion polls show Lebed is a favourite to succeed Yeltsin in the event of the president being unable to carry on in office due to ill-health.
It is unclear how Lebed will act at the heart of an alliance whose generals were his Cold War foes during most of his more than 20-year army career and which he still depicts as hostile.

Moscow says NATO's expansion to take in former members of the now defunct Soviet-led Warsaw Pact would threaten Russian security interests. Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary are top of the waiting list to join.
At a time when some other Russian leaders are treading softly over NATO, Lebed has pushed himself into the front line, firing salvo after salvo against its expansion plans.
Last year he described the North Atlantic Treaty Organisaton as a "big drunken hooligan in a kindergarten who says he will hit anyone he likes".

In a newspaper interview last month Lebed threatened economic sanctions against Germany and the United States if NATO expanded but later disowned the comment. On Tuesday, he said expansion could provoke a "hot or cold war".

Lebed has repeatedly proved that he is ready to speak his mind and does not fear controversy since Yeltsin brought him into the Kremlin last June as a reward for finishing third in Russia's presidential election on June 16.
In Brussels he will be on a diplomatic mission and may be constrained by the need to reflect an official position.
But Lebed's diplomatic skills are unproved, and he could be stepping out of the frying pan into the fire after a dramatic week in which he has faced hostility at almost every turn.
He was jeered and branded a traitor in parliament on Wednesday over the terms of a peace deal which he signed on August 31 to halt the fighting in breakaway Chechnya.
Yeltsin finally backed him over the deal on Thursday and rejected talk of him quitting over another issue, but then told him to buckle down and work more closely with the government.

Such a reprimand might apply over NATO, but the issue is hazy. Lebed's attacks are out of step with recent remarks by Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov, who has said expansion is unavoidable and Russia should start preparing for it.

But Yeltsin and Defence Minister Igor Rodionov have in the past week both called for NATO to reach agreement with Russia before pushing ahead with expansion. Moscow's repeated threat, if it is ignored, is unspecified "adequate" measures.
